sections.h2: Washington real estate excise tax rates
sections.html:
Washington charges a graduated state excise tax on each sale of real property. It starts at 1.1 percent of the selling price and rises to 3 percent on the top slice. The rates come from RCW 82.45.060. Each rate applies only to the part of the price inside its band, so a sale is never taxed at 2.75 percent across the board.

The dollar thresholds are adjusted every fourth year. The Department of Revenue shows one set of band limits for sales through the end of 2026 and a new set for sales beginning January 1, 2027, so a closing in December 2026 and one in January 2027 use different numbers.

State ratePortion of price, through Dec. 31, 2026Portion of price, from Jan. 1, 2027
1.1%Up to $525,000Up to $551,000
1.28%$525,000.01 to $1,525,000$551,000.01 to $1,551,000
2.75%$1,525,000.01 to $3,025,000$1,551,000.01 to $3,051,000
3.0%Over $3,025,000Over $3,051,000

Land classified as agricultural land or timberland is taxed at a flat 1.28 percent state rate instead. The county assessor assigns that classification, and the buyer must state that the land will keep qualifying use.

sections.h2: Who pays and when it is due
sections.html:
The seller pays. RCW 82.45.080 makes the tax the seller's obligation, and the buyer becomes responsible if the seller doesn't pay. The tax goes to the county treasurer in the county where the house sits and is due on the date of sale, even if the deed is recorded later.

The date of sale is the day the deed is signed and delivered to the buyer or the buyer's agent. The Department of Revenue treats that as the notary date unless someone can prove a different one. Timing matters because of these rules in RCW 82.45.100:

  • Tax not paid within one month of the sale starts to carry interest from the date of sale.
  • A penalty of 5 percent applies after one month, 10 percent after two months and 20 percent after three months.
  • The penalties can be collected from the seller only.
  • If the tax is late, the buyer is personally liable unless a document showing the sale is recorded in the county's property records.

The interest rate is 6 percent for 2026 and for 2027. In practice an escrow or title company takes the tax out of the seller's proceeds at closing, so most sellers never write a separate check.

sections.h2: Local tax on top of the state tax
sections.html:
Yes, there is one. The local tax is calculated separately and added to the graduated state rate for the total due. Under RCW 82.46.010, a county or city may impose a tax of up to 0.25 percent of the selling price, and may impose an additional tax of up to 0.5 percent in lieu of a different local option listed in RCW 82.14.030(2).

The local rate follows the location code of the property, and the code can differ between an incorporated city and the unincorporated county around it. Ask the county treasurer or your escrow officer for the exact combined rate before you settle on a net-proceeds number. Local revenue pays for capital projects such as streets, parks and water and sewer systems.

Washington allows only a limited list of exemptions, and only one can be claimed per transfer. The exemption code goes in section 7 of the affidavit, and the seller should keep the paperwork that proves it. The rules sit in chapter 458-61A of the Washington Administrative Code. These come up most often for homeowners:

  • Inheritance or devise. WAC 458-61A-202 exempts transfers by will or inheritance, with or without a mortgage attached. A later sale by the heir is taxable on the full price. An heir who buys out siblings with cash owes tax on that cash.
  • Gifts. Under WAC 458-61A-201, a gift with no consideration is not a sale. If the person receiving the house takes over the mortgage payments, that counts as consideration and the debt is taxed. Both parties sign a supplemental statement.
  • Foreclosure transfers. WAC 458-61A-208 exempts trustee's sales, court-ordered mortgage foreclosure sales, sheriff's sales on a judgment, and deeds in lieu of foreclosure when no extra consideration passes.
  • Condemnation. A sale to a government under written notice of eminent domain is exempt under WAC 458-61A-206.
  • Bankruptcy. Transfers by a trustee after a confirmed chapter 11 or 12 plan are exempt under WAC 458-61A-207.

An ordinary arm's-length sale of a house, including a sale of an inherited or distressed house, fits none of these. It is taxed on the full selling price.

The seller files a real estate excise tax affidavit with the county treasurer, along with the deed and the payment. A deeded transfer goes to the treasurer of the county where the property is located. Mailing the affidavit and deed to the Department of Revenue by mistake can delay the filing and cause penalties and interest. Forms are on the Department of Revenue site.

The right affidavit depends on the property. A single location affidavit covers one or more parcels inside one local jurisdiction code. A multiple locations affidavit with a worksheet is needed when parcels sit in different jurisdiction codes, even inside one county. An agent for the seller or buyer can sign it, and electronic signatures count when proper authentication is used.

Keep records that support the price and any exemption for at least four years. All sales are subject to audit, and under RCW 82.45.100 the Department generally can't assess or refund more than four years after the sale unless there was fraud, a misstatement of a material fact or a failure to report the sale. A refund request is also due within four years and goes through the county treasurer for a deeded transfer.

sections.h2: If the tax is never paid
sections.html:
Unpaid tax can become a lien on the property, and the state has two ways to collect from the seller. Under RCW 82.45.080 the Department of Revenue may bring an action of debt against the seller, or may proceed the way a lender would in a mortgage foreclosure, and using one route doesn't rule out the other. The Department also audits transactions after the fact and assesses additional tax with interest and penalties if a price was understated or an exemption was claimed without support.

Controlling interest transfers have their own rule. When 50 percent or more of an entity that owns Washington real estate changes hands within 36 months, the Department treats it as a sale of the real property, and the return is due within five days of the transfer. Anyone selling a house held in an LLC or partnership should call the Department's REET team before moving ownership interests.

Before closing, ask the escrow officer for a written estimate of the state and local excise tax so it shows on the settlement statement. Confirm the sale date, since the one-month clock starts there. If you claim an exemption, bring the proof: letters testamentary or a death certificate for an inheritance, or the signed supplemental statement for a gift. After closing, make sure the affidavit went to the county treasurer and keep your copy. A cash sale doesn't change any of this. The tax is the same, but the closing is usually quicker, so the payment from your proceeds happens sooner.

faqs.q: Does the buyer or the seller pay the Washington real estate excise tax?
faqs.a: The seller pays. State law makes the tax the seller's obligation, and the buyer becomes responsible only if the seller fails to pay. In most closings the escrow company deducts it from the seller's proceeds and sends it to the county treasurer.

faqs.q: How is the state tax figured on a higher-priced home?
faqs.a: Each rate applies only to the slice of the price inside its band. The first slice is taxed at 1.1 percent, the next at 1.28 percent, and so on up the table. Local tax for the city or county is added on top, so ask the treasurer or escrow officer for the final figure.

faqs.q: Do I owe the tax if I give my house to a family member?
faqs.a: Not if it is a true gift with no payment or debt assumption. A gift needs a supplemental statement signed by both parties. If the person receiving the house starts paying your mortgage, the Department of Revenue treats the debt as consideration and taxes it.

faqs.q: How long do I have to pay before penalties start?
faqs.a: You have one month from the date of sale. After that, interest runs from the sale date, and penalties of 5, 10 and 20 percent apply at one, two and three months. The penalties are collected from the seller only.

faqs.q: Is an inherited house taxed when it passes to the heirs?
faqs.a: No. A transfer by will or inheritance is exempt, even with a mortgage on the property. The exemption ends when the heir sells to a third party, because that sale is taxed on the full price. Letters testamentary or a death certificate support the claim.
